result: HCV remains a significant global health burden with 3-4 million new infections annually, 60-80% progressing to chronic infection among ~71 million chronically infected individuals. In the United States, acute HCV incidence has increased >133% over the past decade, associated with the opioid epidemic, and reinfection remains a concern even after treatment.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C49-C50 are all supported by appropriate citations to published literature. These claims provide epidemiological context from prior work and are appropriately referenced, establishing the public health significance of HCV research.

result: HCV exhibits restricted host tropism, robustly infecting only human and chimpanzee hepatocytes in vivo, which has hindered development of immunocompetent animal models. In murine cells, HCV faces barriers at entry (overcome by expressing human CD81/OCLN or adapting virus to murine CD81) and replication (improved by disrupting innate immunity or using selectable replicons), with low-level assembly/release achieved by providing NS2/structural proteins in trans with ApoE overexpression.
evaluation: Claims C4-C11 summarize well-established prior work on HCV host range restrictions and efforts to overcome them in murine systems, all supported by appropriate citations. This provides essential background for understanding the rationale of the current study.

result: Poor HCV replication in murine cells may result from incompatibility of murine orthologs of vital replication host factors with viral machinery. Three host factors have extensive experimental evidence for roles in HCV replication: CypA, PI4KA, and miR-122, though miR-122 is highly conserved between humans and mice.
evaluation: Claims C12-C14 establish the rationale for focusing on CypA as a potential species-specific restriction factor. C12 is speculative but reasonable, C13 is well-supported by citations, and C14 correctly notes miR-122 conservation, logically excluding it as an explanation for species differences.

result: CypA is an 18 kDa cytosolic peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase that binds cyclosporin A (CsA) and has been implicated in various diseases and viral life cycles. CypA was recognized as critical to HCV replication through knockdown experiments and CsA derivative assays, with its PPIase activity intimately linked to this function. SNPs in the CypA coding region (outside the active site) that reduce intracellular CypA levels are associated with an HCV non-permissive phenotype.
evaluation: Claims C15-C22 provide comprehensive background on CypA biology and its role in HCV replication, all supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. This establishes the biological rationale for investigating CypA orthologs as potential determinants of HCV host range.

result: CypA interacts with multiple HCV proteins (NS5B, NS5A, NS2) through its PPIase activity. For NS5A, CypA promotes isomerization of conserved proline residues contributing to proper folding and RNA-binding capacity. CypA inhibition alters lipid/protein trafficking, abrogates DMV formation critical for replication complex assembly, and affects ER compartments where CypA is localized. Mutations in NS5B and NS5A domain 2 are linked to CsA resistance, and CypA binding may enhance NS5B RNA-binding capacity.
evaluation: Claims C23-C25 and C51-C63 comprehensively describe known CypA-HCV protein interactions and their functional consequences, all supported by appropriate citations. This background establishes the mechanistic importance of CypA for HCV replication and provides context for interpreting species-specific differences.

result: Human, chimpanzee, bonobo, gorilla, olive baboon, and rhesus macaque CypA are 100% identical at the amino acid level. Pigtailed macaques express a TRIM5-CypA fusion. Several NHP species appear resistant to HCV in vivo, but rhesus and pigtailed macaque hepatocytes support HCV in vitro, with replication enhanced by Jak inhibition in rhesus cells. Tree shrews have also been proposed as a potential HCV model with limited evidence.
evaluation: Claims C26-C32 establish the conservation of CypA across species and the variable permissiveness of different species to HCV infection, all supported by sequence data (C26) or appropriate citations (C27-C32). This provides essential context for the comparative analysis of CypA orthologs.

result: Among CypA orthologs tested in Huh7.5-shRNA CypA cells, only orangutan CypA (differing by one amino acid) rescued HCV replication to levels similar to human CypA. Mouse CypA facilitated replication at ~3-4% of human levels (~30-fold decrease). Tree shrew CypA did not significantly increase replication despite being well-expressed. Transduction efficiency was >60% for all constructs, and most orthologs were detected by western blot except squirrel monkey and pigtailed macaque CypA.
evaluation: Claims C33-C36, C77-C80 present the core experimental finding that CypA orthologs differ dramatically in their ability to support HCV replication in human cells. The data are supported by multiple experimental approaches (luminometry, western blot, flow cytometry) shown in Figure 1 and supplements, with appropriate controls and replication.

result: The lack of HCV replication in cells expressing squirrel monkey and pigtailed macaque CypA may be due to improper expression, though it is more likely that antibody reactivity for these orthologs is weaker given robust transduction efficiency and detection of all other variants.
evaluation: Claims C81-C82 appropriately acknowledge limitations in detecting certain CypA orthologs while providing reasonable inference based on transduction efficiency data. The authors appropriately qualify their conclusions about these specific orthologs.

result: Six amino acids differ between human and mouse CypA, none in the CsA-binding site. Human CypA showed significant decreases in HCV rescue efficiency for all single amino acid changes to mouse residues. Mouse CypA with single humanizations at residues 12, 14, 52, or 76 showed replication comparable to human CypA. Triply humanized mouse CypA (T11A/A12V/D14G) rescued replication at levels comparable to human, while triply murinized human CypA showed decreased rescue ability.
evaluation: Claims C37-C42 present the key mechanistic finding identifying specific amino acid residues responsible for species differences in CypA function. The data are supported by systematic mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 2 with appropriate controls, statistical analysis, and structural modeling. The striking phenotypic reversal with triple mutants is particularly compelling.

result: Mutating residue 52 in the triple mutant T11A/A12V/D14G did not have a significant synergistic effect on HCV replication.
evaluation: Claim C83 is supported by experimental data in Figure 3b showing that combining the S52C mutation with the triple mutant does not further enhance rescue efficiency, indicating that residues 11, 12, and 14 are the primary determinants.

result: Murine CypA does not exhibit a dominant negative effect on HCV replication when co-expressed with human CypA.
evaluation: Claim C43 is supported by the dual transduction experiment shown in Figure 4b, where cells expressing both human and mouse CypA maintained high levels of infection comparable to human CypA alone. This rules out a dominant negative mechanism and supports a simple incompatibility model.

result: Triply humanized mouse CypA supports HCV spread and infectious particle release as efficiently as human CypA, as assessed by NS5A staining over time and infectivity of supernatants. Mouse CypA rescue showed significantly higher NS5A+ cells than non-rescued controls but lower than human or triply humanized mouse CypA. Parental Huh7.5-shRNA CypA cells showed minimal increase in infectious particles over time but still produced some particles above background.
evaluation: Claims C44, C84-C86 demonstrate that the identified CypA mutations affect not just replication but also viral spread and particle production, supported by NS5A flow cytometry (Figure 5b) and infectivity assays (Figure 5c). The data show appropriate time course analysis and controls.

result: Clone 8 cells (engineered Hep56.1D cells expressing human HCV entry factors, miR-122, and SEC14L2) demonstrate sustained de novo HCV replication compared to parental Hep56.1D cells, regardless of mApoE presence. Replication was consistently highest in Huh7 cells, with ~3-log difference from Clone 8 cells by 6 dpi. Parental Hep56.1D cells showed no de novo replication after first wash at 2 dpi, and mApoE addition did not impact Clone 8 replication kinetics.
evaluation: Claims C45, C88-C90 characterize the engineered murine hepatoma cell line, supported by kinetics data in Figure 6e and expression verification in Figure 6b-d. The data demonstrate successful engineering of a murine cell line supporting sustained HCV replication, though at lower levels than human cells.

result: In Clone 8 + ApoE cells, addition of murine CypA increases HCV replication, with human CypA producing even greater increases. Addition of any CypA construct tested resulted in significant increases in luciferase activity, with human or triply murinized human CypA showing the greatest effect.
evaluation: Claims C46-C47 and C91 demonstrate that CypA overexpression enhances HCV replication in murine cells, supported by data in Figure 7b with appropriate statistical analysis. The finding that human CypA is superior to mouse CypA even in murine cells is consistent with the human cell experiments.

result: Despite elevated replication and mApoE presence in Clone 8 cells, infectious particle production was not significantly greater than parental Hep56.1D cells. Supernatants from Clone 8, Clone 8 + ApoE + human CypA, and Clone 8 + ApoE + triply humanized mouse CypA cells resulted in significantly higher replication in Huh7.5 cells compared to Hep56.1D supernatants, but the increase remained less than one log on average.
evaluation: Claims C48, C92-C93 identify a key limitation: despite improved replication, infectious particle production remains low in murine cells. This is supported by infectivity assays in Figure 7c and appropriately discussed as indicating additional missing factors or inhibitory mechanisms.

result: The phenotypes of the triple CypA mutants in murine Clone 8 cells are reversed compared to Huh7.5-shRNA CypA cells, suggesting the mechanism by which these mutants function may depend on species-specific cellular environment.
evaluation: Claims C69-C70 identify an intriguing context-dependent effect of the CypA mutations, supported by comparing Figure 2e and Figure 7b data. The authors appropriately note this as speculative and an area for future study, acknowledging the complexity of species-specific factors.

result: The cluster of three residues at positions 11, 12, and 14 may play a role in maintaining interactions with HCV replication machinery and/or associating with host factors that facilitate such interactions. The location of these residues opposite the CsA-binding/active site makes it unclear whether changes lead to loss of PPIase activity.
evaluation: Claims C64-C65 are speculative interpretations of the structural location of the key residues. While the structural modeling (Figure 2b) supports their location away from the active site, no direct PPIase activity measurements or interaction studies are provided to test these hypotheses. Additional experiments would be needed to support these mechanistic proposals.

result: Prior work has shown that HCV replication in murine cells requires disruption of innate immunity: full-length HCV replication in primary murine hepatocytes remained low unless MAVS, IRF1, or IFNAR were knocked out; transfection into MAVS-/- MLT cells with miR-122 and human entry factors gave robust replication but infection showed declining replication; and only infection with selectable HCV in Stat1-/- MEFs with entry factors, miR-122, and mApoE showed strong replication and particle production.
evaluation: Claims C66-C68 accurately summarize prior work on HCV in murine cells, all supported by appropriate citations. This provides important context for interpreting the current results and highlights that the authors' approach of not disrupting innate immunity is more challenging but more relevant for developing immunocompetent models.

result: Several speculative explanations are proposed for low infectious particle production in murine cells: a murine inhibitory factor (analogous to tetherin for HIV-1) may require more replication to overcome; the luciferase assay may be too sensitive, detecting replication insufficient for robust particle production; missing or incompatible co-factors/adaptors may be needed to facilitate CypA interactions; and effects observed in hepatoma lines may differ in primary hepatocytes or with patient isolates.
evaluation: Claims C71-C74 are speculative hypotheses about mechanisms limiting particle production in murine cells. While these are reasonable possibilities supported by analogy to other systems (C71 cites HIV-1 tetherin; C74 cites PI4KA work), they remain untested hypotheses requiring future experimental validation.
